excerpts.label: circle formulas
excerpts.text:
### Use the Properties of Circles

Do you remember the properties of circles from [Decimals and Fractions Together](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/5-3-decimals-and-fractions)? We’ll show them here again to refer to as we use them to solve applications.

![An image of a circle is shown. There is a line drawn through the widest part at the center of the circle with a red dot indicating the center of the circle. The line is labeled d. The two segments from the center of the circle to the outside of the circle are each labeled r.](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f=webp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/0d30ec3bb3c6047df7a95520f048c31ffcb49e93)

- 𝑟rr is the length of the radius
- 𝑑dd is the length of the diameter
- 𝑑=2⁢𝑟d=2⁢rd=2r
- Circumference is the perimeter of a circle. The formula for circumference is


𝐶=2⁢𝜋⁢𝑟C=2⁢π⁢rC=2πr

- The formula for area of a circle is


𝐴=𝜋⁢𝑟2A=π⁢r2A=πr2


Remember, that we approximate πππ with 3.143.143.14 or 227227227 depending on whether the radius of the circle is given as a decimal or a fraction. If you use the πππ key on your calculator to do the calculations in this section, your answers will be slightly different from the answers shown. That is because the πππ key uses more than two decimal places.

excerpts.label: rectangle formulas
excerpts.text:
The perimeter, 𝑃,P,P, of the rectangle is the distance around the rectangle. If you started at one corner and walked around the rectangle, you would walk 𝐿+𝑊+𝐿+𝑊L+W+L+WL+W+L+W units, or two lengths and two widths. The perimeter then is

𝑃=𝐿+𝑊+𝐿+𝑊or𝑃=2⁢𝐿+2⁢𝑊P=L+W+L+WorP=2⁢L+2⁢WP=L+W+L+WorP=2L+2W

What about the area of a rectangle? Remember the rectangular rug from the beginning of this section. It was 222 feet long by 333 feet wide, and its area was 666 square feet. See [Figure 9.20](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids#CNX_BMath_Figure_09_04_013). Since 𝐴=2⋅3,A=2⋅3,A=2⋅3, we see that the area, 𝐴,A,A, is the length, 𝐿,L,L, times the width, 𝑊,W,W, so the area of a rectangle is 𝐴=𝐿⋅𝑊.A=L⋅W.A=L⋅W.

![A rectangle is shown. It is made up of 6 squares. The bottom is 2 squares across and marked as 2, the side is 3 squares long and marked as 3.](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f=webp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/d111bb6bb7bfd21bfe84165e6e8059b2bc37df7e)Figure 9.20The area of this rectangular rug is 666 square feet, its length times its width.

- Rectangles have four sides and four right (90°)(90°)(90°) angles.
- The lengths of opposite sides are equal.
- The perimeter, 𝑃,P,P, of a rectangle is the sum of twice the length and twice the width. See [Figure 9.19](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids#CNX_BMath_Figure_09_04_012).


𝑃=2⁢𝐿+2⁢𝑊P=2⁢L+2⁢WP=2L+2W

- The area, 𝐴,A,A, of a rectangle is the length times the width.


𝐴=𝐿⋅𝑊A=L⋅WA=L⋅W

excerpts.label: triangle area
excerpts.text:
![A rectangle is shown. The side is labeled h and the bottom is labeled b. The center says A equals bh.](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f=webp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/0b39686d1ca3b92987ff62d6a54aeb039e46fa0a)Figure 9.21The area of a rectangle is the base, 𝑏,b,b, times the height, ℎ.h.h.

We can divide this rectangle into two congruent triangles ( [Figure 9.22](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids#CNX_BMath_Figure_09_04_036)). Triangles that are congruent have identical side lengths and angles, and so their areas are equal. The area of each triangle is one-half the area of the rectangle, or 12⁢𝑏⁢ℎ.12⁢b⁢h.12bh. This example helps us see why the formula for the area of a triangle is 𝐴=12⁢𝑏⁢ℎ.A=12⁢b⁢h.A=12bh.

![A rectangle is shown. A diagonal line is drawn from the upper left corner to the bottom right corner. The side of the rectangle is labeled h and the bottom is labeled b. Each triangle says one-half bh. To the right of the rectangle, it says “Area of each triangle,” and shows the equation A equals one-half bh.](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f=webp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/ada031efaa56dcfe88ae9731048e9e9d6de335e5)Figure 9.22A rectangle can be divided into two triangles of equal area. The area of each triangle is one-half the area of the rectangle.

The formula for the area of a triangle is 𝐴=12⁢𝑏⁢ℎ,A=12⁢b⁢h,A=12bh, where 𝑏bb is the base and ℎhh is the height.

To find the area of the triangle, you need to know its base and height. The base is the length of one side of the triangle, usually the side at the bottom. The height is the length of the line that connects the base to the opposite vertex, and makes a 90°90°90° angle with the base. [Figure 9.23](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids#CNX_BMath_Figure_09_04_037) shows three triangles with the base and height of each marked.

![Three triangles are shown. The triangle on the left is a right triangle. The bottom is labeled b and the side is labeled h. The middle triangle is an acute triangle. The bottom is labeled b. There is a dotted line from the top vertex to the base of the triangle, forming a right angle with the base. That line is labeled h. The triangle on the right is an obtuse triangle. The bottom of the triangle is labeled b. The base has a dotted line extended out and forms a right angle with a dotted line to the top of the triangle. The vertical line is labeled h.](https://openstax.org/apps/image-cdn/v1/f=webp/apps/archive/20260604.144757/resources/560d38b21417f2bce89db022f3b45456828dd7a7)Figure 9.23The height ℎhh of a triangle is the length of a line segment that connects the the base to the opposite vertex and makes a 90°90°90° angle with the base.

𝑎2+𝑏2=𝑐2a2+b2=c2a2+b2=c2
